 As the month of November begins, so too does open enrollment for Affordable Care Act health insurance plans, but there are a few changes in store this coming year. 
 Higher premiums and new verification rules are shaping this next round of coverage, as the Trump Administration cracks down on fraud with more safeguards. However, those measures could also make it more difficult for people to sign up for coverage.
 WINK Smart reviewed the biggest changes consumers need to know. 
 As far as premiums go, Americans need to brace for more increases coming in 2027. The higher premiums are due to Congress letting enhanced COVID-era federal subsidies for ACA coverage expire at the end of 2025. 
 For context, premiums rose 26% in 2026 and are set to rise again by roughly 15% in 2027. 
 The Trump Administration says the additional security measures implemented will prevent fraudulent enrollments and unauthorized changes to insurance policies. With more scrutiny of consumers and agents, though, the enrollment process may be slower. That is especially true for first-time applicants and those switching states or brokers.
 RELATED: Expired ACA subsidies and insurer disputes threaten SWFL patients 
 According to CBS News, policy experts claim millions of people have dropped or last coverage earlier this year. While those experts blame expired federal subsidies, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy JR points to the crackdown on fraud as the main reason.
 Back in August, the Trump administration canceled policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected of being improperly signed up. CBS News claims a small number of those enrollees have since regained coverage. 
 Going into 2027, certain immigrants will also lose access to ACA subsidies as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed by Congress last year. That stripped subsidy eligibility from certain refugees, asylees, people with Temporary Protected Status, temporary H-1B visa holders, and those with pending green-card applications.
 There are also new rules that extend to brokers in an attempt to protect consumers from unauthorized activity by bad actors. As it is outlined in a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services released, this only affects consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states including Florida. 
 This does not apply to state-based exchanges.
 Consumers using brokers through the federal marketplace now need to authorize a specific agent with a one-time code or link to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. That link or code will be sent via text message, email, or an automated phone call from a private enrollment platform used by the agent. 
 People with incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace or submit an online application to update it.
 The federal government also temporarily barred agents who were not registered to sell ACA coverage until February. That could make finding a broker more difficult during open enrollment.
 The new rules leave consumers weighing tighter enrollment checks alongside higher costs. 
 The open enrollment period began on Nov. 1 with more steps for some shoppers and fewer options for finding a broker. Experts suggest making an appointment with a broker as soon as possible to ensure there is enough time to find a plan that works best for them.
